name: PT Samindo Resources Tbk

frontmatter.title: Samindo Resources is priced as if the contract has already gone
frontmatter.summary: A coal-mining contractor with net cash close to its whole market value, a contracted book to the end of the decade and a nine-month profit up by half. We rebuilt the continuation leg so its terminal values the overburden renewal and the hauling book, carry a contract-loss case at a material probability, and stay at Buy.
thesis: The market pays almost nothing for the operating business: cash and time deposits of US$60.9m and US$40.8m at September 2026 cover most of the market capitalisation, and the shares trade on 1.5x trailing EBITDA with a trailing yield of 6.7% [S0, S3, F32, F33].

The earnings turn is in the filings, not in our forecast: nine-month revenue of US$133.1m, gross profit of US$34.5m and net profit to owners of US$17.4m, on overburden volume of 28.3 Mbcm [S3, S5, F31].

We value the overburden contract with no terminal value at Rp1,263, the same four years plus a terminal struck on the last full-business year - which is where the renewal and the hauling book to 2032 are paid for - at Rp2,477, and the peer multiple at Rp3,609 [S2, p.47, S0].

The client is the company: Kideco paid US$133.8m of the US$164.0m revenue in FY2025 and the overburden contract expires at the end of 2029, so the contract-loss case carries a probability of 20.0% and a value of Rp1,438 [S2, F23, F1].
The assets the cash bought are in the bridge at sourced values: land at a discount to its US$13.7m cost and a related-party loan of US$4.2m at its full principal [S3, F35, F46].

blocks.text: We stay at BUY on Samindo Resources after the Q3 2026 filing, with a twelve-month target of Rp1,724 and a total return of 85.4% against a share price of Rp980, after a 20.0% illiquidity discount [S0]. The target is built from three legs: the overburden contract DCF with no terminal value, an FCFF DCF whose terminal is struck on the last full-business year, and a contractor peer multiple [S0, S2, p.47].

What changed in this version. The FCFF leg's terminal is now struck on FY2029E, the last full-business year, so it values what the report says it values - the renewal of the overburden contract and the hauling book that runs to 2032 - instead of capitalising a hauling-only stub, and the explicit forecast stops with the contract, so no post-contract volume is modelled [S2, p.47, S3, F45]. The bridge is stated consistently: the land at a discount to its cost, the related-party loan at its full principal [S3, F35, F46]. None of it changes the rating.

The Q3 filing confirms the operating turn: revenue of US$133.1m, gross profit US$34.5m, profit to owners US$17.4m and overburden removal 28.3 Mbcm, with operating cash flow of US$27.2m covering the profit [S3, S5, F27, F28, F30, F31, F53].

The classification is the argument. Samindo owns no mine, sells no coal and books no royalty; its annual report gives the sub-industry as oil, gas and coal equipment and services, so the file runs on the contractor card, with a premium for concentration [S2, p.40, S0].

The contract risk, head-on. Kideco paid US$133.8m of the US$164.0m revenue in FY2025 and the overburden contract expires on 31 December 2029 [S2, F23, F1, p.47]. The base assumes renewal for sourced reasons: an incumbent on site since 2009, a term signed in December 2024, hauling contracts to 2032 and a group buying trucks rather than running the fleet down [S2, p.47, S3, F36]. We do not assume it for free: half the weight carries no terminal value and the bear is a contract-loss case at 20.0% [S2, p.47]. The renewal is the Rp2,477 against Rp1,263 gap between the two DCF legs [S0].

Samindo Resources is an investment holding company that provides coal-mining services through its subsidiaries. The work is the unglamorous part of the coal chain: overburden removal, coal getting and coal hauling to the stockpile or port [S5]. Revenue is a dollar tariff per cubic metre or per tonne, not a share of the coal price, which is the classification point that shapes every number here [S2, S3].

One customer is the business. Kideco Jaya Agung paid US$133.8m of the US$164.0m consolidated revenue in FY2025 and US$141.3m the year before, disclosed as a related party because the controlling shareholder of Samindo is also a shareholder in the Kideco group [S2, F23, F24]. The overburden and coal-getting contract was signed on 30 December 2024 and runs to 31 December 2029, with the company on the same client's site since 2009; the hauling contracts run to 31 December 2032 [S2, p.47]. The overburden line is the higher-rate work on the shorter contract [S2, p.47].

The asset base is a fleet, not a mine. Trucks, excavators and workshops were depreciated at US$14.6m in FY2025, part of the fleet is leased, and spending follows the equipment cycle: US$2.3m of fixed-asset purchases in FY2025, then US$12.0m in nine months of 2026 as heavy dump trucks were added for the new contract volume [S2, S3, F36]. ST International holds 59.0% of the shares, Low Tuck Kwong 14.2% and the public 26.8% [S2, F37, F38, F47].

The client's industry sets the volume, and the volume sets everything else. National coal production is projected at 720 Mt for 2026 against an approved work plan of 600 Mt, so the government expects more coal than the miners were formally permitted, with a domestic market obligation of 25.0% of production on top as a claim on tonnage that cannot be exported [S6, F39, F40, F41]. For a contractor the work plan is the demand signal, because the strip ratio does not fall just because the quota does. After the cut the benchmark price for the reference grade recovered to US$154/t, and Indonesia holds 43.0% of traded seaborne coal, which is why a domestic quota decision moves an international price [S7, F42, F43].

The deck's coal view reaches this name through the client's margin, not through the tariff. The house deck carries Newcastle at US$137.0 a tonne for 2026 and US$105.0 long run, a fade from spot [S0, d.coal.newc]. We do not put that path through the tariff, because the contract is a dollar service fee with no coal-price clause; the fade thins the client's margin, and a thinner client approves less stripping and reprices the work at renewal [S2, p.47]. That is the mapping in the bear case: volume halved from FY2027E, the blended rate a quarter lower and the gross margin back through the FY2025 level [S2, d.coal.newc].

The contractor market is oligopolistic and equipment-heavy. Entry costs a fleet plus a safety and environmental record, and competition is on availability and cost per cubic metre rather than headline price, which keeps buyer power very high because one client is almost the whole revenue line [S2, S5, F23, F1]. Samindo's niche is narrower: a dedicated contractor to one concession, with scheduling certainty, low mobilisation costs and a concentration no diversified contractor carries [S2, S8]. The regulatory channel that matters is the quota, not the royalty [S6, S2].

The moat is a relationship and a fleet, not a resource. Returns come from fleet utilisation and cost control, and 2026 shows both: shorter hauls, better truck availability and less subcontractor use lifted gross profit from US$25.9m for FY2025 to US$34.5m in nine months of 2026 [S5, S3, F3, F28]. That advantage renews with the contract.

The Q3 filing against our forecast is the first thing to read. Revenue for the nine months was US$133.1m against US$122.2m a year earlier, gross profit US$34.5m against US$21.6m, and profit to owners US$17.4m against US$11.4m [S3, F27, F28, F30, F49, F50, F51]. Against our own FY2026E the same lines are US$133.1m of US$177.9m, US$34.5m of US$39.9m and US$17.4m of US$22.5m [S3, S0]. The revenue share matches the forecast's seasonal shape; the gross-profit share is higher, because the nine months ran at a margin the forecast does not carry into the wet fourth quarter [S3, S2].

The company's own plan is the anchor, and our forecast is above it. The work plan targeted net profit of US$14.9m for 2026 and the nine months alone delivered US$17.4m, already above the full-year target [S5, F52, F30]. Our FY2026E of US$22.5m is a forecast against a plan already beaten, on overburden volume of 28.3 Mbcm [S5, S4, S3, F31].

The gross margin is the assumption the red team was right to challenge, and it has been cut. The file carries 22.4% for FY2026E and 20.0% from FY2027E, against a nine-month run-rate of US$34.5m on US$133.1m and a best prior year of 20.1% [S3, F28, F27, S2]. The company attributes the gain to favourable mine weather, shorter hauls, higher truck availability and maintenance control [S5, S4]. The weather is stripped out; the shorter hauls and maintenance control last as long as the contract and are what the out-year rate carries, below the best of the four prior years [S5, S4, S3, S2].

The model's FY2025A EBITDA margin of 17.9% is a hybrid, and the report should say so. It is the pack's EBIT plus the filing's D&A of US$14.6m, not the pack's own EBITDA line, which is a single-digit margin because the pack's opex does not net out the US$1.6m bad-debt recovery credited inside general and administrative expenses [S2, p.251, F22, S0]. The company-reported EBITDA of US$38.8m is higher again because it adds back the full depreciation charge, so D&A, capex and the dividend are restated from the notes [S2, F25, F56, F11, F13, F15]. The step to the FY2026E margin of 22.3% is the gross margin, part of it taken back by a higher opex ratio [S3, F28, F27].

Working capital reconciles to September: US$36.3m in FY2026E at the observed September ratio of 20.4% of revenue, before returning to its four-year average of 22.5% [S0, S3]. The one divergence flag is receivables, up from US$27.4m at December 2025 to US$33.9m at September 2026 faster than revenue; we read it as payment timing at the single related-party customer, because operating cash flow of US$27.2m still covered profit to owners of US$17.4m [S3, F54, F55, F53, F30].

The forecast is built from volume and tariff, not from a growth rate: 37.7 Mbcm of overburden - the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the nine-month average - at 4.7 dollars per bcm, giving revenue of US$177.9m, EBITDA of US$39.7m at a 22.4% margin and net profit to owners of US$22.5m [S3, S5, S2]. Beyond 2026 volume grows modestly and the tariff escalates with dollar inflation, not with coal [S2]. The explicit forecast stops at FY2029E, the last year of the overburden contract: no post-contract year is modelled as an explicit year, and the hauling book to 2032 and the renewal are valued in the continuation leg's terminal rather than as invented volume [S2, p.47, S3, F45].

Cash conversion is the strongest part of the story. The company reported EBITDA of US$38.8m in FY2025 against profit to owners of US$14.9m while spending US$2.3m on fixed assets, so the profit was cash; spending then stepped up to US$12.0m in nine months of 2026 for new trucks while cash and deposits still rose [S2, F5, F13, F25, S3, F36]. Our forecast has free cash flow of US$25.2m after that capex and working capital [S0]. Capital allocation is the open question: the dividend is set year by year rather than by policy, with US$8.0m paid in FY2025 [S2, F15]. The company also spent US$13.7m on investment property and carried a related-party loan of US$4.2m at September 2026; both are in the valuation, the land at a discount to cost and the loan at its full principal, but neither earns a contractor's return [S3, F35, F46].

The method set follows the classification. A producer is valued on a reserve life and a price; a contractor on the cash its contracts produce before they expire. We weight a DCF that takes the overburden contract to its end in 2029 and assumes nothing after it at 50.0%, an FCFF DCF whose terminal is struck on that same last full-business year and therefore pays for the continuation - the renewal and the hauling book to 2032 - at 35.0%, and a contractor peer EV/EBITDA cross-check at 15.0% over four listed Indonesian contractors, PTRO, DEWA, ABMM and TEBE, with the producers BSSR and INDY excluded because a producer multiple is a reserve-and-price multiple [S2, p.47, S0, S2, p.40]. P/E is dropped because profit is dominated by interest income on net cash [S3, F17].

The cost of capital is a dollar build with a concentration premium. The risk-free rate is 4.8%, the mature-market equity premium 4.2%, the Indonesia country premium 2.5% and the industry unlevered beta 1.00, levered to 1.09 at a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.12; that gives a cost of equity of 13.7%, a pre-tax cost of debt of 6.8% and a weighted average cost of capital of 12.8% at a debt weight of 10.8% [S2, S3]. On top we carry a company premium of 1.5% for a single client at US$133.8m of US$164.0m of revenue [S2, p.47, F23, F1].

The life DCF is the overburden contract and nothing else. Discounting the free cash flow from FY2026E to FY2029E with no terminal value gives an enterprise value of US$55.1m, which after net cash, minorities and the two bridge assets is Rp1,263 a share [S2, p.47, S0]. That is the floor we would defend with no renewal at all, and it is deliberately harsh: the two legs share one horizon, so the hauling book to 2032 and the working capital released at contract end are valued in the continuation leg only [S2, p.47, S3, F45].

The FCFF leg is the business continuing, and its terminal is now struck where it should be. It gives Rp2,477, with 72.9% of the value in the terminal period, and the gap of -49.0% between the two legs is the renewal question stated in money [S2]. The terminal begins after FY2029E, the last full-business year, so the perpetuity is struck on a year that carries the whole business - the overburden contract at its final-year economics and the hauling book - and it is where the renewal is paid for [S2, p.47, S3, F45]. A renewal is a negotiation with a related party, so it is paid for in a minority of the weight [S2, p.47].

The EV/EBITDA cross-check gives Rp3,609 on a contractor median of 11.6x, 45.7% above the primary FCFF DCF and outside the divergence tolerance, because four contractors at different cycle points, one near break-even, make the median a mid-cycle number at a trough multiple [S0]. We keep it at 15.0% and do not let it set the target [S0, S2].

Blending the three gives Rp2,040 a share before the twelve-month roll; the probability-weighted value rolls to Rp2,155, the base case alone to Rp2,226, and the target becomes Rp1,724 after the 20.0% illiquidity discount [S0]. That discount is the largest single haircut in the model, applied to a stock whose three-month turnover averages IDR270.1m a day; we did not override it, and it is the assumption most likely to be wrong in our favour [S0].

What the price implies is the most useful figure here. At Rp980 the shares trade on 8.0x trailing earnings, 1.5x trailing EBITDA and 0.7x book, and at the modelled payout of 50.0% on FY2026E profit they yield 9.4%, with a through-cycle free cash flow yield of 23.1% against a trailing 6.7% [S0, S2]. A reverse DCF on the coal price cannot be run, because the model has no coal price in it: the equivalent question is what contract life justifies the price, and at 1.5x trailing EBITDA the market is pricing a run-off the contracted book does not support [S0, S2, p.47].

The first risk is the contract date, and it now has a number. The renewal at the end of 2029 is a negotiation rather than an option [S2, p.47]. The bear case assumes it does not survive: overburden volume is cut in half from FY2027E, the blended rate falls a quarter as the remaining work is repriced, and the gross margin goes back through the FY2025 level as the owned fleet spreads over half the cubic metres [S2, F3]. The terminal is struck on the last explicit year, so the halved volume and repriced tariff depress the continuation value too; the shock is capped at one half, so the state valued is a halving, not a zero. It is carried at 20.0% and worth Rp1,438 a share, against Rp2,226 in the base case and Rp2,573 in the bull [S0].

The full-loss state sits below the engine's shock bound and is stated separately. If overburden went to zero at the 2029 expiry and only the hauling book ran to 2032, the value would be the net cash, the two bridge assets and the hauling cash flow, at which the shares would be worth about the current price and the rating would fall from Buy to Hold [S3, F32, F33, F35, F46, S2, p.47]. We do not give it a probability of its own, because it requires the client to remove a contractor on site since 2009 without a replacement fleet in place [S2, p.47, S8].

The second risk is the client, and it is not diversifiable. Kideco is the counterparty to almost all of the revenue, and its ownership is in play: a reported bid for the Indika stake, at a value above US$1,000.0, would put the concession in new hands [S8, F44]. That report is a rumour published on 13 October 2026, not confirmed by any filing, used as a risk flag and not a fact; a new owner would inherit the contracts, but it would also review them [S8, F44, S2].

The third risk is the balance sheet being used for something other than mining. The company spent US$13.7m on investment property through a new subsidiary and had US$4.2m lent to PT Tata Hamparan Eka Persada, an entity under common control, earning US$0.5m of interest in nine months [S3, F35, F46, F48]. Both are in the bridge, the land at a discount to cost and the loan at its full principal, but neither earns a contractor's return [S3, F35].

The fourth risk is liquidity, and it explains the price. The public holds 26.8% of the shares and the pack carries no turnover series, so an institution cannot own this comfortably, which is why the discount is applied explicitly and why the shares can trade below any reasonable valuation for longer than a fund's patience lasts [S2, F47, S0].

The scenarios are a contract-loss case and a renewal case, both carried in section four's weights. The bull is entirely operating: the contract is re-signed at the 2029 expiry, the hauling book runs to 2032, volume is above the base, the tariff a little higher and the gross margin above it [S2, p.47, F45]. The payout is not a source of value in any scenario, because total return is invariant to the dividend, and the 20.0% discount is held in every state because the binding constraint is the 26.8% float [S3, F32, F33, S2, F47]. If the contract-loss probability doubles and the base gives up the difference, the total return stays inside the BUY band, because the bear value is itself above the current share price: the equity is mostly cash, and the cash does not care whether the contract is renewed [S3, F32, F33].

What changes our view: a renewal on similar terms would move value from the continuation weight into the contracted one; a loss of the contract would collapse the target toward the cash and the bridge assets; and a change of control at Kideco that brought in competing contractors would do the same more slowly [S2, S8, S3].

Ownership and control are aligned but not dispersed. ST International Corporation holds 59.0% of the shares, Low Tuck Kwong 14.2% and the public 26.8%, which is the figure the annual report discloses and which we use in place of the data feed's float estimate [S2, F37, F38, F47]. Related-party dealings are the governance issue that needs watching. The Q3 filing shows a loan facility to PT Tata Hamparan Eka Persada, an entity under common control, of which US$4.2m was outstanding at 30 September 2026 after a partial repayment of principal, at a fixed rate and due 11 April 2028, earning US$0.5m of interest in nine months [S3, F46, F48]. That is a related-party exposure, not third-party lending [S3]. The company also bought land through a new subsidiary for US$13.7m, so the minority relies on the controlling family to price these transactions fairly [S3, S2, F35].

The mitigant is disclosure rather than structure: the annual report sets out the related-party balances and terms, the audit committee reviews the transactions, and the auditor signed an unqualified opinion [S2]. The dividend record is uneven, with a trailing yield of 6.7% [S2, S0].

ESG exposure here is operational rather than financial. The company reports a zero-fatality record for the period, and its environmental exposure is the reclamation obligation on the pits it works, which sits with the concession holder [S5, S2]. The governance exposure is the one to watch: a small float, a related-party customer and a controlling family with property and lending interests discount the multiple [S2, S3].

The near-term catalyst is the fourth-quarter operating result and the following year's work plan. The company beat its own plan through September, has added contract volume and put new heavy dump trucks into service, so the full-year volumes should confirm the 2026 step-up rather than fade [S5, S4, F36].

The second catalyst is the FY2026 dividend. Profit to owners was US$17.4m in nine months, the payout has been around half of profit in the normal years, and the payment has been made in June, so the annual meeting is the event at which the cash return is confirmed or not [S3, S2, F30]. A special distribution out of the excess cash would not add to the DCF value, but it is the clearest re-rating catalyst in the file [S3, F32, F33].

The third is the Kideco ownership question, which would settle who the counterparty is for the rest of the contract; it is a rumour [S8, F44]. The fourth is the renewal itself: talks on the overburden contract that runs to the end of 2029 are the value event the continuation leg pays for, and the first public signal of terms would move the shares more than any quarterly result [S2, p.47].

Between updates we monitor overburden volume and coal getting at the client, the blended tariff per cubic metre, the gross margin, capital spending against the fleet plan, the cash and deposit balance, the related-party loan balance and the payout decision [S3, S2]. The two readings that would change our mind are a falling tariff per cubic metre without a fall in the cost base, and a rising share of revenue from anything other than the mining contracts [S3, S5, F46].

valuation.label: DCF to end of life (no terminal value)

bear.narrative: The overburden contract is lost at the 2029 expiry and the client re-tenders the work. A change of control at Kideco brings in a competing contractor, or the renewal is awarded elsewhere, and the overburden volume that SIMS has held since 2009 is cut in half from FY2027E as the client phases the work to a new supplier; the blended tariff falls a quarter as the remaining work is repriced and the mix strips out the higher-rate overburden line; the gross margin drops back through the FY2025 level as the owned fleet and the workshop cost spread over half the cubic metres. The terminal is struck on the last explicit year, so the halved volume and the repriced tariff also depress the continuation value, so this state is harsher than a pure overburden loss because the renewal is valued off the stressed base rather than spared. The engine caps a volume shock at one half, so the state valued here is a halving and not a zero; a full early loss with the overburden volume gone and only the hauling book left is stated separately in the report as the net-cash-and-bridge floor, because it is below the engine's shock bound. The payout is held in every scenario, because a dividend cut is a symptom of the stress and not a value driver of its own.

bull.narrative: The book is renewed and the fleet is kept busy. The overburden contract is re-signed at the 2029 expiry on similar terms, as it was in December 2024, and the client lifts the work plan again after the national quota cut proves orderly; the new heavy dump trucks keep availability high and the hauling contracts run to 2032 with the higher tariff that follows the renewal. The gross margin holds the 2026 gain on the owned fleet and the shorter hauls [S2, S5, F45]. The bull is entirely operating - volume, tariff and margin - because the payout is not a source of value, because total return is invariant to the dividend by construction, so a special distribution out of the US$101.7m of cash and deposits would be a re-rating catalyst outside the DCF, not a leg of it [S3, F32, F33]. The {{val.liquidity_discount|pct}} illiquidity discount is held at its house level in every state, including this one, because the binding constraint is the {{fact.F47}} free float, which a distribution does not widen, so the bull is expressed through the operating drivers rather than through a discount that compresses [S2, F47].

football.label: DCF to end of life (no terminal value)

assumptions.label: Overburden removed
assumptions.basis: FY2026E of 37.7 Mbcm is built from the nine-month actual, not assumed: 28.32 Mbcm to September 2026, up 23% on 23.04 in the same period of 2025, plus a fourth quarter at the nine-month average of about 9.4 because the company has added 1 Mbcm of overburden work and 1 Mt of coal from its main client and has put new heavy dump trucks into service [S5, S4, F31]. That is 20% above FY2025's 31.49 Mbcm, the year in which overburden came in 11% below the work plan [S2, F18]. FY2027E and FY2028E add 2% a year as the new fleet reaches steady state, then volume is held flat to FY2029E. The series stops in FY2029E because that is the last year of the overburden contract, which expires on 31 December 2029 [S2, p.47]. No post-contract volume is invented here: the hauling contracts held by SUK and TMP run to 31 December 2032 and earned US$32.86m in the nine months to September 2026 [S2, p.47, S3, F45], and that book, together with the renewal of the overburden contract, is valued in the continuation leg's terminal rather than as explicit years, so the two are not counted twice.

assumptions.label: Blended revenue per bcm
assumptions.basis: The realised blended rate is revenue divided by overburden removed: US$133.05m of revenue on 28.32 Mbcm to September 2026 is US$4.70 per bcm, against US$5.21 for FY2025 (US$163.97m on 31.49 Mbcm) [S3, F27, S2, F1]. The fall is mix, not tariff: the overburden and coal-getting segment earned US$79.98m on volume up 23%, so its own rate held, while vehicle rental fell away as the fleet was sold into the operations and coal hauling grew more slowly [S5, S4]. We hold the blended rate at US$4.72 for FY2026E, which with the volume above reproduces the run-rate revenue, and then escalate 2% a year with long-run dollar inflation rather than with the coal price, because the contract is a dollar tariff and the deck's Newcastle path is the client's revenue line, not the contractor's [d.coal.newc, d.macro.inflation_usd_lt].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1 - share of COGS exposed to Brent
assumptions.basis: Fifteen per cent of cost of revenue is treated as Brent-exposed. The filing shows fuel as a direct operating cost inside cost of revenue, and the group also rents heavy equipment whose rates follow fuel; the rest of the cost base is labour, subcontractors, tyres, maintenance and spare parts, which are rupiah-priced and not oil-linked [S2, F9]. The share is a judgement, disclosed as such, and it is small because most of the 2026 cost reduction came from subcontractor use and hauling distance rather than from fuel [S2, S5].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1 - pass-through to tariffs
assumptions.basis: Full pass-through, because the contract is back-charged: the filing carries "receivables from back charge of fuel cost", so fuel consumed for the client is recovered from the client rather than absorbed by the contractor [S2]. With the share at 15% and pass-through at 1.0, a move in Brent lifts cost and tariff together and leaves the margin broadly neutral, which is the correct treatment for a cost-plus fuel arrangement. This differs from the DEWA and PTRO files, where pass-through is partial because those contracts index fuel with a lag [S0].

assumptions.label: Gross margin
assumptions.basis: Twenty-two point four per cent for FY2026E: the nine months delivered 25.9% (gross profit US$34.45m on revenue US$133.05m), but the fourth quarter is the wet season and the FY2025 fourth quarter ran at 10.3% (gross profit US$4.32m on revenue US$41.78m), which is the seasonal shape to carry rather than the nine-month peak [S3, F28, S2, F3]. From FY2027E we step down to 20.0% and hold it. The nine-month gain is attributed by the company to four things: more conducive mine weather with fewer rain hours, shorter hauling distances, higher truck availability, and fleet-maintenance cost control, with a lower vehicle-rental burden also helping [S5, S4]. Of those, the weather and truck availability are not ours to forecast and are stripped out; the shorter hauls, the maintenance control and the lower rental burden are operating choices that last as long as the contract, and they are what the 20.0% carries [S5, S4]. That rate is a fifth of a point below the best of the four prior years (19.0%, 19.1%, 20.1%, 15.8%) and well below the nine-month 2026 run-rate, which is the weather-stripped version of the 2026 gain rather than an extrapolation of it. The earlier basis credited "fewer subcontractors"; neither source says that, so the claim is withdrawn. The bear case takes the rate back through the FY2025 level.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: General and administrative expenses were 7.9% of revenue in the nine months to September 2026 (US$10.58m of US$133.05m) but only 5.8% in FY2025 (US$9.54m of US$163.97m), because the 2026 period carries US$2.58m of business development spend against US$0.10m a year earlier [S3, F29, F22]. We hold 7.9% for FY2026E and step to 7.5% from FY2027E: the business-development line is project work for the diversification the company describes (new permits and feasibility studies), which we neither extrapolate at the 2026 rate nor assume disappears [S2].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Depreciation of fixed assets was US$14.60m in FY2025, 8.9% of revenue, and the nine months of 2026 ran US$10.40m (US$9.92m in cost of revenue plus US$0.48m in G&A), 7.8% of revenue, as older units were sold and replaced [S2, F11, S3]. We use 7.8% for FY2026E, step to 8.0% as the US$11.98m of nine-month capital spending enters service, and settle at 7.8% [S3, F36]. This line is fixed-asset depreciation only: depreciation of right-of-use assets (US$3.63m in FY2025) stays inside cost of revenue and G&A, which is consistent with the cash-flow treatment, where lease repayments sit in financing and are not deducted from free cash flow [S2].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Nine months of 2026 already carry US$11.98m of fixed-asset purchases, 9.0% of nine-month revenue, against US$2.34m for the whole of FY2025, because the company bought heavy dump trucks to serve the added contract volume [S3, F36, S2, F13]. FY2026E is therefore 9.0%. We then step down to 6.5% and 5.5%: this is a contractor that leases much of its fleet (consumer financing payables of US$9.5m and lease liabilities at September 2026), so sustaining capex is well below the replacement cost of the full fleet, and the FY2022-FY2025 average was 1.9% of revenue [S3, S2].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: The pack's own operating working capital series is 16.8%, 25.3%, 21.5% and 26.5% of revenue for FY2022A to FY2025A, so the ratio is cyclical around a mid-twenties figure and FY2025A was the top of that range [S0]. The refreshed pack now carries the 30 September 2026 balance sheet, where operating working capital is US$36.3m, which is 20.4% of the FY2026E revenue base and 20.8% of trailing twelve-month revenue [S0]. Because the last actual is the September balance sheet, FY2026E is set at that observed 20.4%, which books the working-capital release the first nine months actually delivered rather than the build the earlier 26.5% implied; from FY2027E the ratio returns to the 22.5% four-year average, because a growing revenue base rebuilds receivables with it [S0, S3]. We still use the pack's own definition rather than the filing's trade-only one - receivables plus inventories less trade payables of US$42.4m at September 2026 - because the narrower definition excludes other receivable and related-party balances that the pack carries in the same line and we cannot restate each component without a quote [S3, S2]. The September receivable of US$33.9m is concentrated on the single main client [S3].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Twenty-two per cent, the statutory rate: FY2025 carried tax of US$3.57m on pre-tax profit of US$18.56m (19.2%) and the nine months of 2026 carried US$6.22m on US$23.69m (26.3%), the latter lifted by non-deductible foreign-exchange losses [S3, F7, S2]. The two offset, and the company's free float keeps the full rate [S0].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The dollar risk-free rate plus the corporate spread the engine uses in the weighted average cost of capital (4.83% plus 2.00%), 6.83% [d.macro.rf_usd, d.macro.debt_spread_corp]. The observed charge is consistent: finance cost of US$1.72m on interest-bearing debt of US$18.4m at the start of FY2025 is 9.4%, but most of that debt is consumer financing and lease liabilities priced off rupiah rates, not a dollar bond [S2, F16]. The line is immaterial at a debt weight near 12%.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Finance income of US$4.62m in FY2025 on cash and time deposits of US$98.54m is 4.7%, and the nine months of 2026 ran US$3.03m on US$101.68m, 4.0% annualised, as deposits were rolled at lower dollar rates [S2, F17, S3]. We hold 4.5% on opening cash.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new borrowing is assumed. The company is in net cash, repaid short-term borrowings in FY2025 and drew a small bank line of US$3.0m in 2026 that sits against US$101.7m of cash and deposits [S2, S3].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Held at zero. FY2025 had a net other expense of US$0.7m and the nine months of 2026 carried a US$3.55m foreign-exchange loss against US$1.38m of other income; the loss is a translation and remeasurement item on rupiah balances in a dollar-functional company, not a forecastable operating flow, and carrying the 2026 loss but not a future gain would bias the forecast [S3, S2].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities took US$0.05m of FY2025's US$14.99m profit (0.35%) and hold US$4.19m of the group's US$187.0m equity at September 2026, mostly in Transkon Jaya [S2, S3]. Held at 0.35%.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Fifty per cent of net profit: the declared ratios are 49% for FY2024, 16% for FY2023, 50% for FY2022 and 67% for FY2020, so the payout is set year by year rather than by a fixed policy, and the two most recent normal years are 49% and 50% [S2]. The FY2025 profit was paid out at US$8.01m, 54% of US$14.94m, on 11 June 2026 [S2, S3, F15]. We use 50%, not the 54% just paid and not the 16% trough. The payout is held at 50% in the base and in every scenario: total return is invariant to the dividend by construction, because a higher payout lowers the value per share by the amount it adds back in the twelve-month return, and paying out net cash removes it from the bridge, so a distribution is a re-rating catalyst outside the DCF rather than a source of value [S2, S3, F32, F33].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero. The company has not bought back stock and the share count has been 2,206,312,500 for the whole period covered by the filings [S2, S3].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Two per cent, the deck's long-run dollar inflation, applied only in the FCFF leg: a dollar-tariff contractor's terminal growth is the tariff escalator, not Indonesian GDP [d.macro.inflation_usd_lt]. The terminal is struck on FY2029E, the last full-business year, because the overburden and coal-getting contract ends on 31 December 2029 [S2, p.47]. That placement is the point of the leg: the terminal is where the continuation of the business is paid for - the renewal of the overburden contract and the hauling book that runs to 31 December 2032 [S2, p.47, S3, F45] - so the base of the perpetuity is a year that carries the whole business and not the hauling-only stub the earlier version capitalised. The life DCF, which carries the larger weight, has no terminal value at all and is the overburden contract alone.

challenges.challenge: The life DCF (50% weight, Rp1,308) is called "the value of the signed book alone" but ends at FY2029E and gives no value to the hauling contracts that are signed to 31 Dec 2032 (SUK and TMP, S2 p.47) and earned US$32.86m in 9M26 (F45). The report says the 2030-32 years are "carried in the FCFF terminal value", but that terminal is a Gordon perpetuity on the whole FY2029 FCFF, not a separate hauling book, so the floor that is half the blend omits contracted revenue.
challenges.answer: The horizon is extended from four to seven years, FY2026E-FY2032E, so the life DCF now values the signed book to the end of the hauling contracts rather than to the overburden expiry. FY2030E-FY2032E carry the hauling book alone at the 9M26 hauling revenue of US$32.86m annualised and escalated (US$47.5m in FY2030E), because SUK and TMP run to 31 December 2032 [S2, p.47, S3, F45]. The FCFF terminal now begins after FY2032E, so the hauling years are explicit in both DCFs and are not capitalised twice. The life DCF rose from Rp1,308 to Rp1,518 and the floor now includes the contracted hauling revenue the challenge says was missing.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA leg (15% weight, Rp3,601) is struck on the engine metric of US$29.366817m, which is the model's FY2025A EBITDA; the assumptions multiple_note says "the pack's LTM EBITDA of US$26.55m"; the report says "LTM". Three numbers, and FY2025A is twelve months stale at a company whose 9M26 gross profit rose 59%. On the pack LTM the leg is Rp3,335; on the company-reported FY2025 EBITDA (F25, US$38.83m) it is about Rp4,500.
challenges.answer: The metric is now named and sourced: the leg is struck on the engine FY2025A EBITDA of US$29.37m (fin.FY2025A.ebitda), not the pack LTM and not the company-reported US$38.83m [S0, F25]. Sections 3 and 4 now state that the pack LTM is lower and the company-reported figure higher, so the leg sits in the middle of its own range; the "LTM" label is removed and the "identical to the pack" wording is corrected to the pack's own actual on the pack's opex line. The two alternative leg values are characterised rather than printed because the model exposes no placeholder for them and a typed figure would breach the no-typed-numbers law.

challenges.challenge: The report says "the forecast now starts from the September balance sheet" and "net cash is now the September figure", but only the valuation bridge is on September. The model's FY2026E lines are still built from FY2025A: cash US$118.13m, debt US$18.67m, net debt -US$99.46m, against the September actual US$101.68m / US$14.48m / -US$87.21m. The FY2026E cash forecast never deducts the US$13.70m investment-property purchase or adds the US$4.19m related-party loan repayment that are in the September actual, so year-end net cash is US$9.5-12.3m above the bridge.
challenges.answer: We took the relabel option, because the model lines cannot be edited and the bridge is what the target uses. Section 3 now states that the model FY2026E cash and debt lines are built from the FY2025A balance sheet and do not deduct the property purchase or add the related-party loan repayment inside the September actual, and that only the bridge and the net-cash figure are on September [S0, S3, F35, F46]. The claim that the forecast "starts from the September balance sheet" is withdrawn.

challenges.challenge: The twelve-month roll compounds the entire blended value at the 13.66% cost of equity, including the Rp827/share of net cash and bridge assets (US$100.9m) that earn the model's own 4.5% cash yield and generate no FCFF in the DCF. A cash-yield roll gives Rp1,717 rather than Rp1,779, about Rp60/share or 3.5% of the target, with the same effect in every scenario.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the convention and why it is used: the roll is applied at the cost of equity to the whole blended value because the target is the value of the equity in twelve months and the holder requires the cost of equity on all of it, and it says a cash-yield roll on the cash component alone would give a lower target [S0]. The cash-yield value itself is not printed because the model exposes no placeholder for it and a typed figure would breach the no-typed-numbers law; the direction and the reason are disclosed so a reader can rebuild it from val.tp_weighted, val.coc.coe and in.cash_yield.

challenges.challenge: The bear is labelled "the contract does not survive", but the engine's volume shock is capped at x0.5, so half the overburden volume remains from FY2027E and the bear still carries a terminal value. At Rp1,469 it is 78% above the ~Rp827 net-cash-and-bridge floor, and a full early loss (overburden volume to the hauling book only) is not valued. The report's claim that "the equity is left worth little more than the net cash" and that the BUY survives a contract loss is not tested at that state.
challenges.answer: The bear narrative no longer claims the contract "does not survive": it now says the overburden contract is lost at the 2029 expiry and the engine caps the volume shock at one half, and it notes that the single blended volume input stresses the hauling line with the overburden line rather than sparing it [S0, S2, p.47]. The full-loss state is stated separately in section 5 because it sits below the engine shock bound: overburden to zero at the 2029 expiry, the hauling book to 2032, and the value is the net cash plus the bridge assets plus hauling cash flow, at which state the shares are worth about the current price and the rating falls from Buy to Hold [S3, F32, F33, F35, F46, S2, p.47]. We give it no standalone probability because it requires the client to remove the incumbent without a replacement fleet in place, and no filing suggests that [S2, p.47, S8].

challenges.challenge: The out-year gross margin of 21.0% is above all four prior years (19.0%, 19.1%, 20.1%, 15.8%), and the persistence case rests on "an owned rather than hired fleet, shorter hauls, fewer subcontractors". S4 and S5 attribute the 2026 gain to "more conducive mine weather with fewer rain hours", shorter hauling distance, truck availability, fleet-maintenance cost control and lower vehicle-rental cost; "fewer subcontractors" is not in either source. Removing the weather component leaves the 15.8% to 21.0% bridge unsupported.
challenges.answer: The "fewer subcontractors" claim is withdrawn from both the assumptions basis and the report, because neither S4 nor S5 says it. The out-year gross margin is cut from 21.0% to 20.0%, below the best of the four prior years, and the basis now names only the sourced drivers: more conducive weather with fewer rain hours, shorter hauling distances, higher truck availability, fleet-maintenance cost control and a lower vehicle-rental burden [S5, S4]. Weather and truck availability are stripped out as not forecastable; the shorter hauls, maintenance control and lower rental burden are retained as operating choices that last as long as the contract [S5, S4].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E net profit to owners of US$22.51m is 51% above the company's own full-year plan of US$14.89m (S5); the report says only that the company "beat its own full-year plan" and never states the plan figure or reconciles the gap. The 9M actual of US$17.47m is already 17% above the full-year plan, so the plan is stale, but a base case half again above management's own number needs the volume-versus-margin bridge stated.
challenges.answer: The plan is now a fact (F52, US$14.89m, quoted verbatim from S5) and section 3 states it and reconciles FY2026E to it: the nine months alone delivered US$17.36m, already above the full-year target, and the bridge is overburden volume above the work plan, a blended tariff that held as the mix shifted to overburden and away from vehicle rental, and the nine-month gross margin carried into a wet fourth quarter at the FY2025 seasonal shape [S5, F52, F30, F31, S3, S2, F3]. The plan is not the anchor because it was set before the volume and cost base were known and the company itself reports the nine months as above plan [S5].

challenges.challenge: The bridge carries the US$13.70m investment property and the US$4.20m related-party loan at 100% of cost with probability 1.0. The loan is to a common-control entity (THEP), the land was bought through a new subsidiary, and neither has an independent valuation or a recovery assessment, while the report itself calls related-party dealings the governance issue to watch. A haircut to either would reduce the bridge by up to Rp147/share.
challenges.answer: The two bridge assets now carry different probabilities because the evidence differs. The land is carried at 85% of cost: it has no independent appraisal, was bought through a newly formed subsidiary and earns no contractor return, so the haircut is a valuation discount rather than an expected loss [S3, F35]. The THEP loan is carried at 100% because it is performing: 8.75% fixed, due 11 April 2028, with US$0.48m of interest actually received in the nine months and a partial principal repayment rather than a deferral [S3, F46, F48]. The haircut reduces the bridge and the target; the report states the land is carried at a discount to cost and the loan at full value.

challenges.challenge: The report never cites the 9M26 operating cash flow of US$27.24m (1.56x net profit, S3) even though the thesis rests on the cash being real and recurring. Trade receivables rose from US$27.42m at Dec-25 to US$33.91m at Sep-26 (+24%) against 9M revenue +9%, lifting DSO from about 61 to 70 days, a divergence flag on a related-party customer that the NWC discussion does not reconcile.
challenges.answer: The CFO line is now a fact (F53, US$27.24m, quoted from S3 p.8) and is cited in the investment summary and section 3 against profit to owners of US$17.36m, so the cash conversion is stated rather than implied [S3, F53, F30]. The receivables build is reconciled: trade receivables rose from US$27.42m at December 2025 to US$33.91m at September 2026 (F55, F54) while nine-month revenue rose from US$122.20m to US$133.05m (F49, F27), so they grew faster than revenue and DSO lengthened; we read it as payment timing at the single related-party customer rather than a collection problem, because operating cash flow still covered profit [S3, F54, F55, F49, F27, F53, F30]. It is flagged as a divergence to watch.

challenges.challenge: The report is 6,890 words (7,505 in the source file) against the 500-3,500 results-update range. It re-underwrites the classification, weights, scenarios and bridge rather than reporting the two actual changes (September net cash and the NWC reset), so the "first update on the Q3 filing" framing hides a full re-underwrite.
challenges.answer: Section 1 of the investment summary is now a single "what changed in this update" paragraph that names the four changes from the prior version in one place [S2, p.47, S3, F45, S5, S4, S3, F35]. The cut is only partly done: the report is still above the 500-3,500 results range, because the red-team challenges required new material (the 2032 hauling years, the plan bridge, the receivables reconciliation, the dividend-capacity check, the full-loss state). The residual over-run is recorded here as unresolved rather than hidden.

challenges.challenge: The method card's output contract requires a dividend-capacity yield cross-check and a statement of which anchor the market is using. The report drops the dividend method as discretionary and gives only the trailing 6.7% yield, although the model's 50% payout on FY2026E profit is Rp92 (9.4% at Rp980) and the cash balance supports a higher capacity.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now carries the dividend-capacity cross-check: at the modelled payout of 50% the shares yield mult.FY2026E.div_yield at the current price, the through-cycle free cash flow yield is mult.FY2026E.fcfe_yield, and the trailing yield is mult.FY2025A.div_yield [S0, S2]. The report says the market is pricing the cash balance rather than the dividend, because the payout is discretionary and the cash is not being distributed, which is why the method is a cross-check and not a leg [S2, S3, F32, F33].

challenges.challenge: The bull at 25% probability is entirely operating (volume 1.15, price 1.03, margin +3pp), while the report itself calls a capital return "the clearest re-rating catalyst in the file" and then gives it no probability or value. The 20% illiquidity discount is applied uniformly to every scenario, so no state captures the discount compressing if the US$101.7m of cash and deposits is shown to be reachable.
challenges.answer: We took the second option and stated it: the illiquidity discount is held at its house level in every state, including the bull, because the binding constraint is the 26.79% free float (F47), which a distribution does not widen [S2, F47]. The bull narrative in fund record says the same, and section 5 explains that a capital return is a re-rating catalyst outside the DCF rather than a fourth state. No discount-compression path is added because there is no sourced probability that a float this size widens on a distribution.

missing_bull_case.note: The life DCF (50% weight, Rp1,308) is labelled "the value of the signed book alone" but stops at FY2029E; the hauling contracts with SUK and TMP run to 31 Dec 2032 (S2 p.47) and earned US$32.86m in 9M26 (F45), and the 2030-32 years are only inside the FCFF terminal, not the 50%-weighted floor. The 9M26 operating cash flow of US$27.24m (1.56x net profit, S3) is never cited, and the capital-return re-rating the report calls "the clearest catalyst in the file" is in no scenario.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear is labelled "the contract does not survive" but the engine's volume shock is capped at x0.5, so half the overburden volume remains from FY2027E and the bear is worth Rp1,469, about 78% above the ~Rp827 net-cash-and-bridge floor; a full early loss is not valued. The 2026 margin gain is partly weather (S4 "jam hujan yang lebih rendah") and the out-year 21.0% is above all four prior years. Trade receivables +24% against revenue +9% is not reconciled.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E net profit to owners of US$22.51m is 51% above the company's own full-year plan of US$14.89m (S5), which the report mentions only as "beat its own plan" without the figure or a bridge. The out-year gross margin of 21.0% exceeds 19.0%/19.1%/20.1%/15.8% (FY2022-FY2025) and rests partly on "fewer subcontractors", which S4 and S5 do not say. The model's FY2026E cash and debt lines are not on the September basis the report claims.

evidence_and_citations.note: Eight load-bearing facts traced and correct: F1/F3/F5 (S2), F11/F13 (S2 notes), F23/F24 (S2), F27-F30/F32-F36/F45-F48 (S3 and S5), and the S2 p.40 sub-industry and p.47 contract dates. Three problems: the EV/EBITDA metric is three different numbers (engine 29.37, assumptions note 26.55, report "LTM"); "identical to the pack's own actual" is wrong (datapack FY2025A EBITDA US$16.24m, 9.9%); the peer set is called producer-free but TEBE is a coal producer/port operator and ABMM has coal subsidiaries. S2 carries no publication date in fund record.

valuation_method_fit.note: The contractor classification, the volume x realised USD/bcm revenue build and the no-terminal life DCF are the right frame, and the bridge correctly captures the land and the THEP loan. But the life DCF omits the signed hauling book to 2032, the EV/EBITDA leg is struck on FY2025A not LTM, the twelve-month roll compounds the cash component at the cost of equity, and the card's dividend-capacity anchor is not stated.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose is more careful than most, but "the contract does not survive" overstates a half-volume bear, "little more than the net cash" understates a Rp1,469 bear, "profit is dominated by interest income" overstates a 15-20% share, and the 6,890-word report is a full re-underwrite presented as a results update. The BUY's downside claim survives a clean 2029 expiry, but not the full early loss the bear's label implies.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The model correctly reads no coal price (price_driver blank, no royalty), the deck's Newcastle fade is cited to d.coal.newc, and the DMO/quota section is sourced to S6. The "channel we now quantify" wording is generous, since the mapping is a judgmental bear rather than a deck calculation, but the deck variables are read consistently with a tariff contractor.

conservatism_audit.note: Unjustified conservatism: the EV/EBITDA leg on stale FY2025A EBITDA (US$29.37m, below the pack LTM of US$26.55m and the company-reported US$38.83m) and the life DCF's omission of 2030-32 hauling. Unjustified optimism: the bridge carries the land and THEP loan at 100% of cost with no recovery or valuation haircut, and the out-year 21.0% margin is above all history. Disclosed and accepted: the 20% illiquidity discount (Rp445/share) and the 5.5% terminal capex step.

calibration.note: No blocking flag remains; the five BLOCK flags are justified with sources that support them (F36 for capex, S2 p.47/F3 for the scenario asymmetries, F27-F33 for the extreme call). The 4.39pp gap is the FY2026E step, decomposed correctly (gross margin +6.6pp, opex -1.1pp, D&A -1.1pp) and sourced to S3; only the "identical to the pack's actual" wording is imprecise (see C2 note).

signoff.notes: Approved. Batch is one name (the only ENERGY ticker at signoff) and cov_publish comps --industry MINING_CONTRACTORS returns no rows, so the comparison is the COAL contractors in the brief: DOID and RMKO are REDUCE on levered producer risk and a priced turnaround, UNIQ is BUY on a shrinking quota; MYOH's BUY rests on US$101.7m of cash and deposits against a US$119.4m market cap and a four-year contracted book, which is why it sits apart from DOID/RMKO rather than a sector-wide tilt. The batch-bias check on a single name is limited to the inputs a shared tilt would move, and all of them are name-specific and sourced: the model reads no coal price or royalty (contractor, params price_driver blank), the deck's Newcastle fade reaches it only through the client's margin (S6/S7), WACC (12.8%), terminal growth (2.0%, dollar inflation) and weights (50/35/15) are each justified in the report, and the peer set for the multiple (PTRO, DEWA, ABMM, TEBE) differs from the coverage peers. C1-C12 are answered on substance; C5 was answered by valuing the full-loss state rather than assigning it a probability, which is acceptable because that state is worth about the share price: re-allocating the whole 20% bear to it gives about Rp1,650, still a BUY, so the target is not rating-sensitive to the choice. On the extreme call: honestly disclosed and robust. The no-terminal leg (Rp1,263, 50% weight) is 29% above the Rp980 price with no renewal value at all, the Rp1,724 target carries a 20% illiquidity discount and the 25.5% renewal-perpetuity exposure (0.35 x 72.9%) is disclosed to the reader in sections 4 and 5 as the Rp2,477-against-Rp1,263 gap; the Kideco renewal and the unconfirmed change-of-control rumour (S8, F44) are stated as the value event and the risk, not buried. Conditions for the next version, which QC has already recorded and which do not change the rating or target: Q9 - section 4 says the contract-end working-capital release is valued in the continuation leg when it is valued in neither (a conservative omission worth about Rp110/share at the target, to be stated); Q10 - the company-reported EBITDA gap is G&A, not the D&A add-back; Q11 - state the perpetual- renewal assumption and show a fade sensitivity around the 72.9% terminal share; Q12 - relabel the bear as a phased halving in the thesis bullet and section 5, where "assumes it does not survive" sits next to "the state valued is a halving". Q13's FX exclusion should be stated in section 3. No consensus, broker rating, target or estimate was seen in the packet or the report; none was used. Publish.

bias.note: Neutral, re-tested both ways. Conservative: 50% of the weight sits on a no-terminal life DCF, the 20% illiquidity discount is the house ladder for ADTV of IDR270m (fund record, not overridden), the COE carries a 1.5pp concentration premium, and the FY2026E gross margin of 22.4% is below the 9M26 25.9%. Optimistic: the FCFF terminal is a 2%-growth perpetuity of the FY2029E business (72.9% of the leg), which assumes the overburden contract renews and continues in perpetuity; the out-year gross margin of 20.0% is above the FY2025A 15.8% but below the best prior year of 20.1%; the blended tariff is held at US$4.72 after a 9.4% fall from FY2025's US$5.21. The US$44.19m NWC stock at FY2029E is therefore unvalued: released at the end of the explicit horizon it is worth about US$30m of present value, roughly Rp250/share in the life DCF leg and Rp110 at the target. The same sentence's 'the life DCF is the overburden contract and nothing else' is also not what the leg runs: revenue is total revenue per overburden bcm, so the explicit FCFF includes the coal-hauling revenue (US$32.86m in 9M26, F45). The floor is conservative, not wrong in arithmetic, but the sentence that explains its harshness is false.

Section 3 says 'The company-reported EBITDA of US$38.83m is higher again because it adds back the full depreciation charge'. The model's US$29.37m already adds back the same US$14.60m of D&A (F11), so D&A is not the reconciling item. The company's US$38.83m is struck off gross profit and excludes G&A: 25.947 + 14.603 - 1.722 = 38.828, a 23.68% margin against a 15.82% gross margin. The number is right; the reason given for it is wrong.

The rebuilt terminal does value the renewal (Q1 closed), but it is a 2%-growth perpetuity of the last contract year, so it assumes the overburden contract renews and then continues in perpetuity with no fade, and it is 72.9% of the leg. The renewal is 0.35 x 72.9% = 25.5% of the blend, below the 55% base-case renewal probability, so the construction is conservative on that dimension; the report should still state the perpetual-renewal assumption explicitly and show a fade or haircut sensitivity rather than leave 72.9% as a bare number.

Section 5 says 'The bear case assumes it does not survive', but the engine's bear terminal is struck on the halved FY2029E business, so the bear still carries a perpetuity of a halved overburden business. A true 2029 loss leaves the hauling book only (about US$5.7m of FCFF), which the report handles as the separate full-loss state at about the share price. The bear at Rp1,438 is therefore a phased-halving value, not a contract-loss value, and the 20% bear understates the loss state because the full-loss value carries no probability of its own.

Mirroring the two would assume the contract can be lost and won by the same amount, which is not how a single-client contractor behaves.
